---
title: "Brokerage without bridging"
subtitle: "The middle class does not connect rich and poor in Brazilian cities"
---


::: {.eyebrow}
Main result
:::

::: {.lede}
Whether city dwellers of different means come into contact depends on who stands
between them. We looked for those intermediaries in 3.1 billion mobile-phone calls
across nearly 300 Brazilian cities.
:::

::: {.finding}
**No stratum bridges the income poles.** No income group is over-represented on the
routes linking the poorest and the richest residents, and removing the middle class
cuts their reach to one another no more than removing the same number of people at
random.
:::

::: {.finding}
**Apparent elite gatekeeping is a volume effect.** The rich appear to control access to
their own group until the volume of contact between groups is held fixed. Then the
effect disappears, in every city and at both ends of the income distribution.
:::

::: {.finding}
**Intermediation is assortative.** Across every pair of income strata, residents broker
contact more often than chance only when the two people they connect belong to the same
stratum. The intermediate broker that the bridging account predicts is enriched in
none of the 71 cities.
:::

## What this means for cities

Research on urban segregation has moved from where people live to where they go and
whom they encounter. This result adds a further layer: how contact is arranged.
Residents of these cities do call across class lines --- most two-step chains of contact
link people in different income strata --- but no stratum occupies the positions that
would carry interaction from one class to the next. A city can therefore look integrated
by exposure, or even by its share of cross-class ties, while remaining divided in how
those ties are mediated.
